title: Density Matrices of Pulsed Quantum Light
authors: Joscelyn van der Veen, Daniel F. V. James
abstract: Pulsed light is represented by density matrices whose correlation functions have different properties of stationarity and coherence. We show that these density matrices yield equivalent measurement results after accounting for finite detection times. This in turn reveals a physical meaning to the length of a quantization cavity and explains the origin of the physical spectrum for pulsed light. By generalizing the density matrices for pulsed Gaussian states of light, we can describe pulsed light of varying statistics in the same basis and relate the photocount rate to the pulse spectrum.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework for describing pulsed quantum light using density matrices. It demonstrates that when measured over finite time intervals, different theoretical models of coherence yield the same measurable photocount rates. This resolves ambiguities in the theory by linking the measurable spectrum to the physical properties of the light source.
main_problem: The theoretical description of pulsed quantum light, particularly concerning the role of coherence when moving beyond single-mode fields, needs refinement.
main_result: Accounting for finite detection times makes different theoretical density matrices (based on coherence assumptions) yield indistinguishable measurement results for the photocount rate.
method: The authors use density matrices and calculate photocount rates by time-averaging first-order correlation functions, comparing results for Poissonian and squeezed vacuum states.
model_or_system: The system is pulsed quantum light, often generated by mode-locked lasers, modeled using density matrices ($\hat{ho}$) that account for both stationary and nonstationary field characteristics.
key_observables: Photocount rate ($\omega^{(1)}$) and second-order photocount rate ($\omega^{(2)}$).
important_parameters: Finite detection time ($T$), cavity length ($L$), Poisson rate parameter ($\lambda_k$), and squeezing parameter ($\xi$ or $r_k$).
main_assumptions: The crucial assumption is the finite measurement time, which regularizes the measurement outcomes and leads to the equivalence of different theoretical models.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the difference between a coherent density matrix (pulse train) and a stationary density matrix (field with a pulse spectrum).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by introducing the density matrix formalism for pulsed light, deriving the first-order photocount rate, establishing the equivalence of models under finite measurement time, and finally calculating and comparing the second-order photocount rate for Poissonian versus squeezed vacuum states.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems as it provides a rigorous framework for interpreting measurements on pulsed quantum light, resolving ambiguities in defining coherence in time-varying fields.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. We quantize the electric field in some cavity of length L. A coherent density matrix (a) describes the field as a pulse train where each pulse is separated by a time L/c. A stationary density matrix (b) instead has the field existing at all times but with a spectrum that is the Fourier spectrum of a single pulse in any time period L/c.
